summary: This standards-track document defines IS-IS extensions to support multicast forwarding using Bit Index Explicit Replication. They let routers advertise the information BIER needs.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines the extra records that IS-IS routers exchange so that they can forward multicast the BIER way, where the list of receivers travels inside the packet as a row of bits. Each router announces which bit is its own and which labels it uses, so that the forwarding tables can be built.

questions: what is the bier info sub-tlv
subtitle: The IS-IS advertisements that let routers set up Bit Index Explicit Replication multicast.

tldr.problem: Bit Index Explicit Replication forwards multicast by putting the receivers into the packet as a row of bits, but every router on the way has to know which bit belongs to which receiver. IS-IS had no way to carry that mapping.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a BIER Info sub-TLV for the IS-IS extended reachability TLVs, carrying a topology and subdomain pair, the router's BFR-id, and, in a sub-sub-TLV, the range of MPLS labels it wants for each packet size.
tldr.outcome: The result is that IS-IS can act as the underlay for BIER, telling routers which bit is theirs and which labels to expect. RFC 8401 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9272.

sections.title: What BIER Needs from IS-IS
sections.content:
Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER), defined in RFC 8279, is an architecture where all intended multicast receivers are encoded as a bitmask in the multicast packet header, within different encapsulations. A router that receives such a packet forwards the packet based on the bit position in the packet header, towards the receivers, following a precomputed tree for each of the bits in the packet. Each receiver is represented by a unique bit in the bitmask.

This document presents the necessary extensions to the currently deployed IS-IS for IP to support the distribution of the information needed for BIER domains and subdomains to operate. It defines a new TLV to be advertised by every router participating in BIER signalling.

It defines support for the MPLS encapsulation specified in RFC 8296. Support for other encapsulation types, and the use of multiple encapsulation types, are outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: BIER forwards multicast by putting the list of receivers into the packet as a row of bits. IS-IS is used to tell the routers which bit belongs to which receiver, and this RFC defines the extra IS-IS records that carry that.

sections.title: The BIER Vocabulary
sections.content:
Some of the terminology of RFC 8279 is replicated here and extended by the definitions that follow.

BIER is the overall architecture of forwarding multicast using a bit position. A BFR, a Bit Forwarding Router, is a router that participates in Bit Index Multipoint Forwarding, and is identified by a unique BFR-prefix in a BIER domain. A BFIR, the Bit Forwarding Ingress Router, is the ingress border router that inserts the BitString into the packet, and each BFIR must have a valid BFR-id assigned. A BFER, the Bit Forwarding Egress Router, is a router that participates in Bit Index Forwarding as a leaf; each BFER must be a BFR, and each BFER must have a valid BFR-id assigned. A BFT, the Bit Forwarding Tree, is used to reach all BFERs in a domain.

A BIER subdomain is a further distinction within a BIER domain, identified by its unique subdomain identifier, and a subdomain can support multiple BitString lengths. A BFR-id is an optional, unique identifier for a BFR within a BIER subdomain. An Invalid BFR-id is an unassigned BFR-id, and the special value 0 is reserved for this purpose.

Two more terms describe how the underlay path is worked out. The BAR, the BIER Algorithm, is used to calculate underlay next hops. The IPA, the IGP Algorithm, may be used to modify, enhance or replace the calculation of underlay paths as defined by the BAR value. SPF is the Shortest Path First routing calculation based on the IGP link metric.
sections.plainLanguage: The names to learn are the three kinds of router: the one that puts the bits in, the ones that carry them, and the ones that take them off at the end. Each of them needs a number that says which bit is its own.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document adds an entry to the "Sub-TLVs for TLVs 135, 235, 236, and 237" registry: value 32, named BIER Info.

It also introduces a new registry for sub-sub-TLVs for the BIER Info sub-TLV, called "Sub-sub-TLVs for BIER Info Sub-TLV", created within the "IS-IS TLV Codepoints" registry. The registration policy is Expert Review, and the first defined value is type 1, BIER MPLS Encapsulation.

IANA has also created the "BIER Algorithms" registry within the "Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER)" registry. The registration policies are Standards Action for values 0 to 127, Specification Required for values 128 to 239, and Experimental Use for values 240 to 254. The initial values in the registry are 0, meaning that no BIER-specific algorithm is used, and 255, Reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new lists are created: the type number for the BIER record, the sub-records inside it, and the numbers that say how the underlay path is worked out.

sections.title: Domains, Subdomains and Topologies
sections.content:
An IS-IS-signalled BIER domain is aligned with the scope of distribution of the BFR-prefixes that identify the BFRs within IS-IS. In such a case, IS-IS acts as the supporting BIER underlay. Within such a domain, the extensions defined in this document advertise BIER information for one or more BIER subdomains, each uniquely identified by a subdomain-id. Each subdomain is associated with a single IS-IS topology, which may be any of the topologies supported by IS-IS, and local configuration controls which topology and subdomain pairs a router supports. The mapping of subdomains to topologies MUST be consistent within the IS-IS flooding domain used to advertise BIER information.

Each BIER subdomain has as its unique attributes the encapsulation used and the type of tree it uses to forward BIER frames, which is currently always SPF. In addition, per supported BitString length in the subdomain, each router advertises the necessary label ranges to support it.

BIER information advertisements are associated with a new sub-TLV in the extended reachability TLVs, and BIER information is always associated with a host prefix, which MUST be a node address for the advertising node. If this is not the case, the advertisement MUST be ignored. That gives two restrictions: the prefix length MUST be 32 for an IPv4 prefix or 128 for an IPv6 prefix, and when the Prefix Attributes Flags sub-TLV is present, the N flag MUST be set and the R flag MUST NOT be set. BIER sub-TLVs MUST be included when a prefix reachability advertisement is leaked between levels.
sections.plainLanguage: A BIER domain is the part of the network where the same set of receivers applies, and a subdomain is a further split inside it that uses one IS-IS topology and one kind of forwarding tree. The BIER record always hangs off a single router's own address.

sections.title: Procedures and Conflict Handling
sections.content:
A given subdomain is supported within one and only one topology. All routers in the flooding scope of the BIER sub-TLVs MUST advertise the same subdomain within the same multi-topology. A router receiving an advertisement that does not match the locally configured pair MUST report a misconfiguration, and all received BIER advertisements associated with the conflicting pair MUST be ignored. In the presence of such a misconfiguration this leads to partitioning of the subdomain. The RFC gives the example: the combination of advertisements <0,0>, <0,1> and <2,2> is valid, while <0,0>, <0,1> and <2,0> is invalid, and the advertisements associated with <0,0> and <2,0> must be ignored.

On identifiers, if a BFER or BFIR is configured with a BFR-id then it advertises that value in its BIER advertisements; if no BFR-id is configured, the value "Invalid BFR-id" is advertised. A valid BFR-id MUST be unique within the flooding scope of the BIER advertisements, and all BFERs and BFIRs MUST detect advertisement of duplicate valid BFR-ids for a given topology and subdomain. When such duplication is detected, all the routers advertising duplicates MUST be treated as if they did not advertise a valid BFR-id, which means they cannot act as BFER or BFIR in that pair.

Whenever an advertisement is received that violates any of the constraints defined in the document, the receiving router MUST support logging the occurrence, and the logging SHOULD be dampened to avoid excessive output.

On flooding, it is expected that changes in the BIER domain information advertised by IS-IS occur infrequently. If that expectation is not met for an extended period of time, more than a few seconds of burstiness, changes will increase the number of Link State PDU updates and negatively impact performance in the network. Implementations SHOULD protect against this possibility by, for example, dampening updates if they occur over an extended period of time.
sections.plainLanguage: If two routers disagree about which subdomain they are in, the records are dropped and the group of receivers is split. If two routers claim the same number, neither can be used as a receiver until the clash is fixed.

sections.title: The BIER Info Sub-TLV
sections.content:
All IS-IS BIER information is carried within the TLVs 235 and 237, 135 or 236. The BIER Info sub-TLV carries the information for the BIER subdomains that the router participates in as a BFR, and it MAY appear multiple times in a given prefix-reachability TLV, once for each subdomain supported in the associated topology. It advertises a single topology and subdomain combination followed by optional sub-sub-TLVs.

The fields are short. The BAR field specifies a BIER-specific algorithm used to calculate underlay paths to reach BFERs, and its values come from the BIER Algorithms registry. The IPA field specifies an IGP Algorithm to either modify, enhance or replace the calculation of underlay paths as defined by the BAR value, and its values are from the IGP Algorithm registry. The subdomain-id is the unique value identifying the BIER subdomain. The BFR-id is a 2-octet field encoding the BFR-id as documented in RFC 8279; if no BFR-id has been assigned, the value of this field is set to the Invalid BFR-id, which is defined as illegal in RFC 8279.

The use of non-zero values in either the BAR field or the IPA field is outside the scope of this document. If an implementation does not support the use of non-zero values in these fields but receives a BIER Info sub-TLV containing them, it SHOULD treat the advertising router as incapable of supporting BIER.
sections.plainLanguage: The record says which subdomain the router is in, which number it uses, and, for now, two fields that must be zero and are kept for future algorithms.

sections.title: The BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-Sub-TLV
sections.content:
This sub-sub-TLV carries the information for the BIER MPLS encapsulation, including the label range for a specific BitString length for a certain topology and subdomain. It is advertised within the BIER Info sub-TLV and MAY appear multiple times within a single BIER Info sub-TLV.

Two rules govern repetitions. If the same BitString length is repeated in multiple sub-sub-TLVs inside the same BIER Info sub-TLV, the BIER Info sub-TLV MUST be ignored. Label ranges within all BIER MPLS Encapsulation sub-sub-TLVs across all BIER Info sub-TLVs advertised by the same BFR MUST NOT overlap, and if overlap is detected the advertising router MUST be treated as if it did not advertise any BIER sub-TLVs. Label values MUST NOT match any of the reserved values defined in RFC 3032.

The fields carry the maximum Set Identifier used in the encapsulation for this BIER subdomain and this BitString length, with each SI mapping to a single label in the label range: the first label is for SI 0, the second for SI 1, and so on. If the label associated with the Maximum Set Identifier exceeds the 20-bit range, the sub-sub-TLV MUST be ignored. The local BitString length is encoded as per RFC 8296, in four bits, and the label field carries the first label of the range, in twenty bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the BIER record, one sub-record per packet size says which range of MPLS labels the router wants for it. The ranges must not collide, and each size may only be mentioned once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security concerns for IS-IS are addressed in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310.

The Security Considerations section of RFC 8279 discusses the possibility of performing a Denial-of-Service attack by setting too many bits in the BitString of a BIER-encapsulated packet. However, this sort of attack cannot be initiated by modifying the IS-IS BIER advertisements specified in this document. A BFIR decides which systems are to receive a BIER-encapsulated packet, and in making that decision it is not influenced by the IS-IS control messages. When creating the encapsulation, the BFIR sets one bit in the encapsulation for each destination system. The information in the IS-IS BIER advertisements is used to construct the forwarding tables that map each bit in the encapsulation into a set of next hops for the host that is identified by that bit, but it is not used by the BFIR to decide which bits to set. Hence an attack on the IS-IS control plane cannot be used to cause this sort of DoS attack.

While a BIER-encapsulated packet is traversing the network, a BFR that receives one with n bits set in its BitString may have to replicate the packet and forward multiple copies. A given bit will only be set in one copy of the packet, which means that each transmitted replica has fewer bits set, and is targeted to fewer destinations, than the received packet. This is an essential property of the BIER forwarding process as defined in RFC 8279. While a failure of this process might cause a DoS attack, such a failure cannot be caused by an attack on the IS-IS control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: The record only tells the routers where to send packets; it does not tell the sender which receivers to name, so it cannot be used to flood the network.

fields.name: BAR
fields.desc: BIER Algorithm, used to calculate underlay next hops.

fields.name: IPA
fields.desc: IGP Algorithm, may modify, enhance or replace the BAR calculation.

fields.name: subdomain-id
fields.desc: Unique value identifying the BIER subdomain.

fields.name: BFR-id
fields.desc: A 2-octet field; the Invalid BFR-id if none is assigned.

viz.caption: THE ROLES IN A BIER DOMAIN

items.title: BFIR
items.text: The Bit Forwarding Ingress Router inserts the BitString into the packet.

items.title: BFR
items.text: A Bit Forwarding Router, identified by a unique BFR-prefix in the domain.

items.title: BFER
items.text: The Bit Forwarding Egress Router takes the packet off at the leaf.

items.title: BFT
items.text: The Bit Forwarding Tree used to reach all the BFERs in a domain.

items.title: Subdomain
items.text: A further split inside a domain, with its own identifier and packet sizes.

items.title: BFR-id
items.text: An optional unique number for a BFR within a subdomain; 0 means unassigned.
